## Why radar, and why only one night first

eBird (notebooks 02–03) tells us **which species** and **roughly where**.
It can't count birds in the air. Weather radar can: NEXRAD stations scan
the sky every 5–10 minutes, and at night during migration much of what they
detect is birds. The vol2bird algorithm (Dokter et al. 2011) separates the
bird signal from rain and turns it into a **vertical profile**: how dense
the birds are at each altitude, and which way and how fast they're moving.

Radar can't tell species apart, so the two sources complement each other:
eBird says *who*, radar says *how many and when*.

**This notebook processes ONE night at ONE station.**:

- each scan is ~10–20 MB, so a full night at one station is ~1–2 GB;
- processing is slow on a laptop (seconds per scan);
- we want to confirm the method works and the numbers look sane before
  scaling to more nights and stations.

This is also the most 'big data' part of our project, so record the file
counts, sizes and run time here. They go into the report's Database
Management section.

```{r setup}
source(here::here("R", "config.R"))

library(bioRad)     # NEXRAD download + profile tools (uses vol2birdR inside)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)
```

## Choose the night

```{r params}
# --- Edit these to pick a different station / night ---------------------
station <- "KNKX"   # San Diego (see RADAR_STATIONS in config.R)

# Radar files are timestamped in UTC. In late April San Diego is on PDT
# (UTC−7), so the local night of Apr 27 runs from about 02:30 UTC to
# 13:15 UTC on Apr 28. The NEXRAD archive covers any past date, so spring
# nights are available even though we're working in the fall.
#
# FIRST RUN: keep this to a 2-hour window around the usual peak (roughly
# 10 pm – midnight local = 05:00–07:00 UTC) so it finishes quickly.
# ONCE IT WORKS: widen it to the full night, e.g. 01:00 to 14:00 UTC.
date_min <- as.POSIXct("2026-04-28 05:00", tz = "UTC")
date_max <- as.POSIXct("2026-04-28 07:00", tz = "UTC")

# Pick a night with good migration: check the BirdCast Migration Dashboard
# (https://dashboard.birdcast.info) for San Diego County and choose a night
# with a big total. Avoid nights with rain at the station; vol2bird filters
# rain, but heavy rain still degrades the estimates.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
```

## Step 1 · Download the raw scans from AWS

```{r download}
# NOAA publishes the full NEXRAD archive on AWS as open data (no account
# needed). bioRad lists the files for this station and time window and
# downloads them into data/raw/radar/YYYY/MM/DD/STATION/.
# data/raw/ is git-ignored: these files are big and anyone can re-download
# them, so they don't belong in the repo.
t0 <- Sys.time()
download_pvolfiles(
  date_min  = date_min,
  date_max  = date_max,
  radar     = station,
  directory = PATHS$radar
)

files <- list.files(PATHS$radar, pattern = paste0("^", station),
                    recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)
# NEXRAD also publishes small "_MDM" metadata files alongside the scans;
# they aren't radar volumes, so drop them.
files <- files[!grepl("_MDM$", files)]

# Big-data bookkeeping for the report.
tibble(
  scans    = length(files),
  total_mb = round(sum(file.size(files)) / 1e6),
  download_time = round(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "mins"), 1)
)
```

## Step 2 · Turn each scan into a vertical profile of birds

```{r profiles}
# calculate_vp() runs vol2bird on one scan. Key settings:
#   rcs = 11 cm^2   radar cross-section per bird; converts reflectivity into
#                   a NUMBER of birds (see RADAR_RCS in config.R)
#   h_layer / n_layer: 20 layers of 200 m = 0–4 km above the radar, which
#                   covers nearly all nocturnal songbird migration
#   dual_pol = TRUE: uses NEXRAD's dual-polarization data to filter rain,
#                   the main source of false "birds"
# tryCatch() lets one corrupt scan be skipped instead of stopping the run.
t0 <- Sys.time()
vp_list <- lapply(files, \(f) tryCatch(
  calculate_vp(f, rcs = RADAR_RCS, h_layer = 200, n_layer = 20,
               dual_pol = TRUE),
  error = function(e) { message("Skipped ", basename(f), ": ", conditionMessage(e)); NULL }
))
vp_list <- Filter(Negate(is.null), vp_list)

message(length(vp_list), " of ", length(files), " scans processed in ",
        round(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "mins"), 1), " min")

# Stack the individual profiles into one time series (a "vpts" object).
vpts <- bind_into_vpts(vp_list)
```

## Step 3 · Collapse altitudes into nightly migration numbers

```{r integrate}
# integrate_profile() sums each profile over altitude and returns, per scan:
#   vid  birds per km² in the air (density)
#   mtr  migration traffic rate: birds crossing a 1 km line per hour
#        (the standard "how much migration" number; BirdCast uses it too)
#   ff   ground speed (m/s);  dd  direction of travel (degrees, 0 = north)
vpi <- integrate_profile(vpts)

radar_night <- as.data.frame(vpi) |>
  mutate(
    station,
    local_time = with_tz(datetime, "America/Los_Angeles"),
    # Keep only scans taken after sunset and before sunrise at the station.
    # Daytime echoes are mostly insects and would inflate the numbers.
    is_night = check_night(vpi)
  ) |>
  filter(is_night) |>
  select(station, datetime, local_time, vid, mtr, ff, dd)

# Derived summary, small and shareable (raw scans stay in data/raw/).
write_csv(radar_night,
          file.path(PATHS$derived,
                    paste0("radar_", station, "_", format(date_min, "%Y%m%d"), ".csv")))

summary(radar_night[, c("vid", "mtr", "ff", "dd")])
```

## Step 4 · Plot the night

```{r plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5}
p <- ggplot(radar_night, aes(local_time, mtr)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Migration traffic over ", station, " (San Diego)"),
    subtitle = format(date_min, "Night of %b %d, %Y (UTC start)"),
    x = "Local time", y = "Birds crossing 1 km per hour (MTR)",
    caption = "Data: NOAA NEXRAD Level II via AWS; processed with vol2bird / bioRad (Dokter et al. 2011)."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p
ggsave(file.path(PATHS$figures, paste0("04_radar_", station, ".png")),
       p, width = 8, height = 4.5, dpi = 200)
```

## Sanity checks before scaling up

1. **Direction (`dd`):** on a good spring night, most birds should be
   heading roughly north (dd around 315–45°, i.e. NW through NE). Mostly
   southward headings suggest wind-drifted insects or a processing problem.
2. **Magnitude:** compare our peak MTR with the BirdCast dashboard for San
   Diego County on the same night. The units differ (BirdCast reports
   county totals), but busy and quiet nights should line up.
3. **Day-migrant check:** Rufous Hummingbird migrates by day, so it should
   contribute nothing here. If a "night" scan shows big numbers right at
   dusk or dawn, the night filter may need an `offset`.

If all three look right, widen the time window to the full night and add
more nights (e.g. weekly from mid-March to early June). Each night takes the same
code: loop over a vector of dates.
